Today, on Veterans Day, we honor the courage, dedication, and sacrifice of every Virgin Islander who has served our country.

Generations of Virgin Islanders have worn the uniform, serving in every branch and in conflicts around the world, and they continue to serve our community long after they come home. We are proud of them, and we are grateful to their families, who sacrificed alongside them.

Honoring our veterans means more than words. Too many Virgin Islands veterans still have to travel off-island for specialty care, and access to services and benefits in the territory remains a challenge. That’s why I’m committed to strengthening VA care here at home, cutting through red tape, and ensuring every veteran and family receives the care, benefits, and opportunities they have earned.

To every Virgin Islands veteran: thank you for your service. 💙

This November, during Military Family Month, we honor the spouses, children, parents, and grandparents who make sacrifices so their loved ones can serve. They manage households through deployments, distance, and the added challenges of island life, from limited access to services to the long distances between them and military installations on the mainland.

We also recognize the families of our Virgin Islands National Guard, who stand by their loved ones as they deploy overseas and serve our own community through hurricanes and recovery.

Thank you to every Virgin Islands military family. We see you, and we are grateful. 💙

Today and every day, we recognize and celebrate the cultures, histories, and contributions of Indigenous peoples.

Long before these islands were called the Virgin Islands, they were home to the Ciboney, Taíno, and Carib (Kalinago) peoples, who fished our waters, farmed our land, and built thriving communities across St. Croix, St. Thomas, and St. John. Their legacy lives on in our landscape: in the petroglyphs carved at Reef Bay on St. John, in the ceremonial grounds uncovered at Cinnamon Bay, and at Salt River Bay on St. Croix, where Carib warriors stood their ground in 1493 in one of the first recorded acts of Indigenous resistance to European arrival in the Americas.

On Indigenous Peoples' Day, we honor these first Virgin Islanders, whose history is part of our history, and the Indigenous communities whose traditions have endured across generations and continue to shape our territory and our country.

posts.text:
Today, October 1, Virgin Islanders honor Contract Day.

After our ancestors took their freedom from chattel slavery in 1848, the Labor Act of 1849 created a new kind of bondage. Workers were bound to one plantation for a full year, with a day wage and restricted movement, able to change estates only on Contract Day. It was freedom in name only.

On October 1, 1878, when rumors of reform proved false, 30 years of frustration ignited the St. Croix Labor Rebellion, known to us as Fireburn. It was led by four women we revere as our Queens: Mary Thomas, Mathilda McBean, Susanna "Bottom Belly" Abrahamson, and Axeline "Queen Agnes" Salomon.

They demanded fair wages and the repeal of the Labor Act, and many paid with their lives. From their sacrifice came reforms that dismantled the labor system.

Today we honor our heritage and remember their courage. 🔥

Being Caribbean American means carrying two worlds in your heart — and showing up for both. 

This Caribbean American Heritage Month, I'm reflecting on what it truly means to be from these islands and to serve in the halls of Congress. The richness of our culture, our people, our resilience — it shapes everything I do.

Stay with me through the rest of this month as I share what being Caribbean American means to me. ✨

Cicely Tyson didn't just perform — she made a statement every time she stepped on screen.

The daughter of immigrants from the Caribbean island of Nevis, she spent seven decades refusing to let Hollywood define what a Black woman's story could look like. Every role was intentional. Every choice was deliberate. And every performance reminded the world of something it needed to see.

A Caribbean daughter. An American icon. A standard that still stands. 💙

#CaribbeanAmericanHeritageMonth

When the country needed someone to lead the charge on health equity during one of the most critical moments in modern history, a daughter of St. Thomas answered the call.

Dr. Marcella Nunez-Smith has spent her career fighting for the communities medicine too often overlooks — including the Caribbean territories she calls home. Brilliant, dedicated, and rooted in purpose, she is proof that where you come from can fuel exactly the work the world needs from you.

The Virgin Islands raised her. The nation needed her. 💙

#CaribbeanAmericanHeritageMonth

Before there was a blueprint, there was Shirley Chisholm.

The daughter of Caribbean immigrants, she walked into the U.S. Congress in 1968 as the first Black woman ever elected to serve as a Member of Congress— and then dared to run for President four years later. 

She didn't ask for permission. She didn't wait for the door to open. She kicked it down and left it open for everyone who came after.

Unbought. Unbossed. Unforgettable. 💙
#CaribbeanAmericanHeritageMonth

Today, on Veterans Day, we honor the courage, dedication, and sacrifice of every Virgin Islander who has served our country.

Generations of Virgin Islanders have worn the uniform, serving in every branch and in conflicts around the world, and they continue to serve our community long after they come home. We are proud of them, and we are grateful to their families, who sacrificed alongside them.

Honoring our veterans means more than words. Too many Virgin Islands veterans still have to travel off-island for specialty care, and access to services and benefits in the territory remains a challenge. That’s why I’m committed to strengthening VA care here at home, cutting through red tape, and ensuring every veteran and family receives the care, benefits, and opportunities they have earned.

To every Virgin Islands veteran: thank you for your service. 💙
